# RFC 3161 test fixtures

Real timestamp tokens, produced by OpenSSL acting as a Time Stamping Authority.
They are genuine RFC 3161 structures — `openssl ts -verify` accepts them — so
the verifier in `src/rfc3161.js` is tested against real data rather than
against something shaped to match its own assumptions.

Generated offline by `./regenerate.sh`, so the suite needs no network and no
dependency on a third party staying up.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `head.txt` | The data being timestamped, standing in for a chain head |
| `request.tsq` | The `TimeStampReq` for `head.txt` |
| `response.tsr` | Valid RSA-signed token over `head.txt` |
| `response-ec.tsr` | Valid ECDSA-signed token over `head.txt` |
| `response-other.tsr` | Valid token over **different** data (`other.txt`) |
| `response-rogue.tsr` | Valid token from a **different, unpinned** TSA |
| `ca.crt`, `tsa.crt`, `ec-tsa.crt` | The test CA and its signers |
| `rogue-ca.crt`, `rogue-tsa.crt` | An independent TSA we do not pin |

`response-other.tsr` and `response-rogue.tsr` are both *cryptographically
valid*. They exist because the interesting failures are not corrupt tokens —
they are perfectly good tokens that attest to the wrong thing, or that are
signed by someone we have no reason to trust. A verifier that reports those as
VERIFIED is worse than no verifier at all.

## No private keys

Signing keys are generated by `regenerate.sh` and deleted when it finishes. The
suite only ever verifies signatures, so it never needs them, and a project that
argues for careful handling of evidence should not casually ship signing keys.

Everything here is test-only and carries no trust outside this repository.
